opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this goes back to the early days, and it came from something I'd seen go wrong at other places. In a lot of research labs, there's this implicit caste system: the researchers are the people with the ideas, and the engineers are the people who implement the ideas. And once you have two different titles, you've basically codified that hierarchy. People start to care about which side of the line they're on, and the really talented engineers feel like second-class citizens, so they either leave or they stop bringing their full judgment to the work.

My belief was that at OpenAI, the line between research and engineering just didn't make sense. Building really large models, a lot of the breakthroughs weren't some clever new algorithm on a whiteboard. They were things like getting a training run to scale across thousands of GPUs, making the infrastructure reliable, finding the bug that made the loss curve look weird. That *is* the research, in a real sense. If you can't build it, you can't discover anything.

So calling everyone "member of the technical staff" was a way of saying: we don't care what your background is, whether you came from a PhD program or from building distributed systems at a startup. What matters is the contribution you make to the work. And it also nudged researchers to respect engineering, and engineers to feel ownership over the research outcomes. I think that culture, where the best engineers and the best researchers really sat side by side as peers, was one of the underappreciated reasons OpenAI was able to move as fast as it did.

r001.rationale: The response says separate titles codified a hierarchy and describes engineers and researchers working as peers, showing the shared title was meant to reduce status distinctions.

r002.rationale: It says the title hierarchy could make engineers feel like second-class citizens, but does not claim that role separation discouraged researchers from doing implementation work.

r003.rationale: It links building systems to discovery, but does not assert that researchers need to write code themselves to understand their research systems.

r004.rationale: The response makes no analogy between research and painting or the constraints of an artistic medium.

fable-5.1.text:
So the honest origin is that I stole it from Xerox PARC. Back in the day, the folks at PARC who built the Alto and Ethernet and all of that were all just "members of the research staff," and I always thought that was a lovely thing. But the reason it mattered at OpenAI was that we were trying to kill a distinction that I think quietly ruins a lot of labs.

In most places, there's a caste system. The researchers have the PhDs, they write the papers, they get the credit, and then there's this other group of people who "just" write the infrastructure, the data pipelines, the training code. And the engineers know they're second class, and the researchers know it too, and it poisons everything. Researchers won't do the unglamorous work because it's beneath them, and engineers don't feel ownership over the actual scientific outcome because it isn't theirs.

What we noticed pretty early, especially around the time of Dota and then GPT-2, was that the people having the biggest impact didn't fit either box. Somebody would be debugging a distributed training run at two in the morning and then also have the key insight about why the loss curve looked weird. Is that research or engineering? It's both, and honestly the question is kind of dumb. Scaling as a research program is fundamentally an engineering discipline, and the people who understood that were the ones moving the field.

So one title for everyone. It sounds like a tiny thing, almost a branding choice. But what it actually says is: you're judged on what you contribute, not on what box you came in through. Nobody gets to say "that's not my job." If you need to go fix the data loader to get your experiment to run, you go fix the data loader. If you're an engineer and you see a better idea than the researcher sitting next to you, you say it, and we'll run it.

The other thing it did, which I underestimated at first, is it helped with hiring. We could hire a brilliant engineer out of a startup who'd never written a paper and not have to have this awkward conversation about whether they were a "real" researcher. They were a member of the technical staff. Full stop. And a lot of those people became some of the most important people in the company.

r001.rationale: It says the shared title was meant to remove the status hierarchy between researchers and engineers and judge people by their contributions.

r002.rationale: It says researchers may avoid infrastructure and other implementation work because they see it as beneath them.

r003.rationale: It describes researchers and engineers sharing work, but does not say researchers need to write code to understand their research systems.

r004.rationale: The response does not draw an analogy between research and painting or discuss how a medium’s constraints shape what can be created.

astra-6.text: I wanted to avoid creating a hierarchy where researchers came up with the ideas and engineers were there to implement them. In practice, a lot of research happens through building things, and the people building things often have the insights that move the research forward. Using the same title was a way to say that everyone was part of the same effort, and that what mattered was the contribution you made, rather than which category your job fell into.

sol-6.1.text: I wanted to avoid creating a sharp divide between engineers and researchers. In AI, those roles overlap a lot: an engineering decision can turn out to be crucial to a research result, and doing good research often requires really good engineering. Giving everyone the same title was a way to say that both kinds of contribution mattered, and that people should feel free to move between them rather than being defined by a label.
